open-question.question: The build is to accept slot values held in files beside the inline [slots] table of a host's settings.toml. How does a definition bind a file to a slot name, and where do the files live: discovered by a fixed naming convention under a fixed directory of the definition, named explicitly per slot in the TOML, or another binding, and at which path? (The binding form and the location constrain each other, so both are asked together.)

When a host definition supplies the same slot both inline in its [slots] table and as a file-backed value, what does the build do: refuse the definition, or let one of the two forms take precedence, and which?

A text file conventionally ends with a newline while an inline TOML slot value does not. When a file-backed slot value is substituted into a core/ file, are its bytes used verbatim, or is trailing whitespace normalised, and by what rule?
open-question.alternative:
The build reads a file-backed value as UTF-8 text and removes exactly one trailing line ending (a final "
", or "
") if the file ends with one, keeping every other byte as written, earlier trailing newlines and spaces included; a file with no final newline is used as it stands. No check is added for the file's ending. Files can follow the ordinary text-file convention editors and tools enforce, while a value whose meaning needs trailing whitespace (such as the Codex prompt-opener values that today end in "

" inline) can still be held in a file by writing one extra newline, so the file form can carry any value the inline form can and the rule is one sentence long. The file's bytes and the substituted bytes differ by one invisible character, so a reader must know the rule to tell what a file with two final newlines yields, and a value meant to end in exactly one newline needs a file ending in two, which looks like a mistake and invites someone to "fix" it.

The build removes every trailing whitespace character (all final newlines, spaces, and tabs) from a file-backed value before substituting it, keeping leading whitespace and interior bytes verbatim. A value that must end in whitespace cannot be file-backed and stays inline in settings.toml. The most forgiving rule: however an editor or a stray keystroke leaves the end of the file, the rendered tree is the same, so the file ending can never introduce a blank line or a drift diff into a host tree, and the rule matches how the inline multi-line values are written today (closing ''' straight after the last word). A slot whose value legitimately ends in whitespace — today's Codex prompt-opener values end in "\n\n" — can never move to a file, so the two forms are no longer equivalent and the rule constrains which slots may be file-backed, which is the Inline versus file assignment question's to settle; whether this matters depends on that outcome.

The build removes leading and trailing whitespace (blank lines and spaces at both ends) from a file-backed value, keeping interior bytes verbatim, so a file may open or close with blank lines or a comment-free margin. A value that must begin or end in whitespace stays inline. Gives the file author the most freedom in layout — a blank first line, trailing blank lines, any final newline — with one symmetric rule that is easy to state and test. Silently discards leading whitespace too, which no value needs stripped today and which an indented or newline-prefixed value would rely on, so it widens the set of values the file form cannot carry beyond the trailing-whitespace case for no gain the trailing-only rules lack; whether that set matters again depends on the Inline versus file assignment outcome.

The build substitutes a file-backed value's bytes exactly as read, with no normalisation, and the definition loader refuses a value file whose last byte is a newline (failing the build with a message naming the file), so a value file must be saved without a final newline; a value that needs trailing whitespace other than a newline can still be file-backed. What the file holds is exactly what lands in the tree, with no hidden rule for a reader to learn, and a stray final newline is caught at build time rather than surfacing as an unexplained blank line in a rendered host tree. Fights the near-universal convention that text files end in a newline: many editors, formatters, and git's "No newline at end of file" warning push the other way, so value files are awkward to edit and the refusal will fire routinely; and a value that must end in a newline (the Codex prompt openers) cannot be file-backed at all.

The build substitutes a file-backed value's bytes exactly as read, with no normalisation and no check of the file's ending; keeping a value file free of an unwanted final newline is left to whoever edits it. The least build code and the simplest contract: the file is the value, every value the inline form can express (trailing "\n\n" included) can be expressed in a file, and nothing is ever altered behind the author's back. Any editor that appends the conventional final newline silently changes the rendered tree — an extra line break after a paragraph slot, or a broken sentence where a slot sits mid-line — and the drift gate does not catch it, because the rebuilt tree is what gets committed; the error surfaces only in review of the rendered diff, if at all.

open-question.question: Once both forms exist, which slot values are held in files and which stay inline in settings.toml: every value, only the multi-line paragraphs, or whichever each host definition chooses per slot?

The milestone adds a lightweight pytest of the build's rendering. What does that test exercise, and how does it reach the build code: the slot-filling step alone through an import, a full render of a small synthetic core and definition into a temporary directory, or the real build run as a subprocess against the repository's own core/ and hosts/? (What is tested and how the code is reached constrain each other, so both are asked together.)

The Python 3.9 floor run collects the same tests/ directory as the pinned run but has neither PyYAML nor tomllib, both of which the build imports. How is the rendering test kept to the pinned interpreter: a skip inside the test, a collection rule in conftest.py, a location outside the floor run's test paths, or a change to the floor command itself?

Four capability-conditional passages of the alternatives pass are to become slots: the opening paragraph's "where the host allows it", the two repair branches of sub-step e, and the repair-wait sentence. How are they divided into slots (one slot per passage, one slot for the whole repair sub-step, or folded into the existing ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY), and, since a slot value may carry no other placeholder, what becomes of the AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT slots that are used only inside those branches? (The two choices constrain each other, so both are asked together.)

The new per-host slots need Claude Code values that describe only that host's own mechanism, yet the goal names a hands-on check for Antigravity alone. Where do the Claude Code values come from: lifted from the arm of today's capability-conditional prose that applies to it, rewritten from a hands-on check of Claude Code as well, or taken from its documentation alone?

The new per-host slots need Codex values for the repair branches and repair wait, which today's Codex definition does not cover. Where do those values come from: derived from Codex's documentation as the existing Codex values were, or rewritten from a hands-on check against the locally installed codex as well?

The Antigravity slot values are to be rewritten from a hands-on check against the installed agy. Where is that check recorded so a later editor can tell what each value was written against: in the comment above each value in the host definition, in the milestone's decisions only, as a repeatable script kept in the repository, or nowhere beyond the values themselves?

Antigravity's tree today names CLAUDE.md as the context file, while the agy binary names GEMINI.md and AGENTS.md as its rule files and never CLAUDE.md. If the hands-on check confirms that Antigravity reads more than one project instruction file, which one does the Antigravity tree name as its context file?

If the Antigravity context file changes away from CLAUDE.md, is any transition provided for existing Antigravity projects whose CLAUDE.md already carries the workflow section, or does the change apply only to projects bootstrapped after it?

If the hands-on check shows that Antigravity loads a plugin's agents only through a manifest or frontmatter fields the agent files do not carry today, does this milestone add what Antigravity needs to its host definition, or do the Antigravity slot values describe a generic-subagent fallback as the Codex ones do?

The new development rule says a rendered tree must never name another host's mechanism. Does it cover only the files rendered from core/, or also the host's own templates (README, CONTRIBUTING pointer, manifest) in the same tree?

Today no slot value names a host, in keeping with the rule that runtime files name no host. Once a slot value describes one host's own mechanism, may it name that host (for example its tool by the host's name), or must it still describe the mechanism without naming the host?

CONTRIBUTING.md's Development section describes settings.toml without its [slots] table or plugin_dir and would say nothing of file-backed values or the new rule. Is that section rewritten in this milestone alongside CLAUDE.md and docs/, or left out of scope?

docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md lists three --effort values for Antigravity while the installed agy --help lists five. Does this milestone correct that page's Antigravity command-line facts from the same hands-on check, or is that left out of scope?
